Author: @WilVincent27
Content:
One point about artist cancellations, there’s a minimum number of songs / amount of time to be classified as a ‘set’ which some bands do to get around being classified as cancelled. Avenged Sevenfold did this at Leeds one year, playing 5 songs with messed up vocals before calling it a day, and countless bands have finished sets early but meeting obligations if they have issues / the crowd just hate them (Nickelback, Portugal).

Also a lot of the volunteers get in effect free entry, but have to work 8 hours a day, sometimes at stupid hours. For Glastonbury, some get in by volunteering for a charity instead.

In terms of rubbish, there’s normally a cup deposit, which is 10/20p. This is returned if you take your cups back to a specific location (NOT the bar!). This is why you get people with massive cup stacks. It’s an easy way of making money and many don’t care about that 20p, though some play practical jokes on cup collectors (I did it for a few years when I was skint, and it was my way of feeding myself during the festival!). You also used to get a free can of beer for each trash bag returned in the campsite, which was emergency last night refreshment!

There used to be at least one homeless guy in Derby who would save up to get a Download ticket just to collect cups. He said he made more money than selling the Big Issue in Derby itself during that time, which was about 15km from the festival site, but the closest real train station.

Content: I can understand what goes on behind the scenes in organising something as big as this. In 93,  I was the Assistant Event Director for Brisbane's B105 Skyfire. An annual fireworks event on the Brisbane River, Australia. The Director himself was Steve Brown, a brilliant man who had to keep 20 million things in his head at all times. Emergency services, pedestrian traffic, air traffic control, water traffic, the fireworks crew themselves , water traffic, the Royal Australian Air Force, security,  the list was endless. And he had to be aware of what each of them were doing at any instant. Basically,  he was running an entire city by himself, and at the same time,  he was preparing for Peter Gabriel's WOMAD in Adelaide.  A very incredibly talented man. RIP Steve. I still miss you ❤

Author: @tehwabbbit
Content:
5:16 - Unsure about Glasto due to its size, but a lot of festivals are often attended by large catering companies who have *many* different trucks, and appear to to be different businesses but all owned by the same people. I found this accidently when I saw a bunch had the same trading name on their certificates! There are of course independants, but this does skew the argument sometimes that its "good for local economy" when its all facilitated by large nationals and not local catering firms. In fact, a local firm I know enquired and it was really prohibative, whereas these large firms can attend as its all aggregated income, so if one stall doesn't do great its not gonna kill the business.

Also not touched on is usually a set price structure, to avoid undercutting other vendors, which is easier to control when most them are all the same firm! Then there are forced sales, like in the UK the festivals that got sponsored by Liquid Death which meant all vendors had to buy this from the wholesaler and sell only this water at a set price.

Know this is definitely true of at least 2-3 big UK festivals

Content:
I've worked at the festival now for quite a while, and love this video. Knowing the process and background of the event, including writing my dissertation on the event, there is a few things i can confirm. 
- The wonderfully disgusting long drop toilets, are built on-top of large concrete tanks, that are permanently burred underground, when the festival is not operational, large metal covered are placed over the top 
- The site office is open every day in the Green Barn, and staffed by around 30-40 full time staff, who organise the festival. 
- The festival is fairly financially resilient, the festival has significant funds, specifically to ensure the festivals future, alongside owning a local housing estate, that they receive rental income from. They effectively have 3 pots of money, One for the following festival, one for disaster recovery and expansion and one that goes to charity. 
- The festival own the largest onsite recycling center of its type, which processes all festival waste, and recycling
- Glastonbury Festival does not pay artistes the amount they would usually charge, some event put their own money into their performance just to perform at Glastonbury.

Author: @jackspencer7540
Content: Really interesting and well-made video, but a few things stood out to me. It mentions that headliners get paid a lot, but that’s actually not the case at Glastonbury. Artists usually take a much lower fee than normal, often because of the prestige and the festival’s focus on charitable giving. Another major part of the festival that wasn’t mentioned at all is the role of volunteers. Thousands of people work shifts in exchange for a ticket and help keep things running smoothly, including stewarding, welfare support, and litter collection. The bit about long-drop toilets being described as an innovation felt a bit generous as well. They are practical, but not new, and a lot of people find them pretty grim. Also, the video mentions that Glastonbury earns around $80 million, but it’s not clear where that figure comes from. Even if it’s roughly accurate, it’s worth pointing out that Glastonbury is not run as a commercial enterprise in the same way as other big festivals. Most of the profits go to charity, and that’s a huge part of what makes it different. Still, I really enjoyed the video and just thought these points were worth adding!

Author: @n1vg
Content:
I've been to Glastonbury 3 times as crew and Burning Man 13 times and the logistics are (in most ways at least) shockingly different and really shape the two events. Burning Man is 80 miles off the interstate on a dry lakebed with no fixed infrastructure on site and no vending except for ice. They do have to have pump trucks making the rounds constantly for the portable toilets, but mostly participants are on their own for food, water, and trash disposal. Burning Man definitely doesn't have the rule about no timed drinking games - that was definitely something my camp's bar did. But despite lots of free booze and fewer restrictions, the crowd seems not as rowdy as Glastonbury to me. I think it's mostly a matter of density, with Burning Man having 1/3 as many people in a significantly larger area and no giant stages. It's also a longer event and people pace themselves more.

The video briefly mentioned the crew bars, and really that's one of my favorite parts of Glasto. There are *thousands* of people working, performing, and volunteering there and there are six or seven crew bars, cafes with reasonably-priced food, and they have their own little stages and performances. It's like a festival within a festival.

Crew areas also get their own long drops so you don't have to fight the crowds. In fact, if you're there first thing in the morning, the surface of the water below you is still enough that you can see the reflections of all of the other toilets that share the same pit, which is its own kind of special Glastonbury moment.

Author: @benfulford3943
Content:
Great video wendover. Brilliant to see an American channel making a video about the greatest festival in the world. If you haven't already been you should try and go. I guarantee it'll be one of your best weekends while smashing your step count records (it's really hard to get across just how big it is). 
A couple of other really interesting points that you missed that make Glastonbury stand out compared to all other festivals. The first is that it always sells out completely within an hour or so before they've released the line up. Everyone wants to go to it no matter who is playing. However even if you aren't really into any of the acts on the main stages there are up to 2000 acts playing across a hundred or so stages so there will definitely be something there for everyone even if you don't like the headline acts. 
The other major point that I think would be most interesting to this channel is the majority of the profits are donated to charity. This means that they pay considerably below market rates to the artists who play. Famously the rolling stones never played because they always wanted a million pound to headline whereas the organisers refused to pay anyone that much and ended up being considerably less than that. For a lot of artists it is such an honour to play they take a big pay cut. The fact that it is all played live on the BBC and iPlayer meaning they get incredible exposure helps as well

Author: @xjdisuehd
Content:
A classmate of mine in high school sets up their stall at this festival, selling margs and Mexican snacks/food. She moved to UK after getting married and operates a small Mexican food place on London outskirts. When we visited her in UK, she showed us one strategy that really helps with business there

- Advertise well in advance on social media.
- Make sure you take cash and your prices are in round figures. For example, £5/£10. Limit your portion sizes or make them larger and use round figures, VAT and local taxes if any. Figure out everything, including your margin in advance.
- Keep change with you, especially coins. She typically gets about £4000-ish worth of change for the festival in coins, and another £2000 worth change in smaller bills. This typically lasts the entire festival, and makes her offerings more accessible and attractive.
- Sometimes there are problems with card payments and mobile payments due to the extreme strain on local internet networks (wireless and wired - wherever available), but cash still works.

We're planning to go there, hopefully in 2027 - 2026 is farming year.

Well, this video was a surprise!

Author: @Bill_N_ATX
Content:
I’ve worked at many festivals across the US, working audio for both the festival and for third party broadcasters, like SiriusXM and other Terrestrial Radio stations and streaming platforms. I’ve been at well ran festivals where artists, their crew, and the local show crew were able to quickly and efficiently do their jobs to put in a great show for the customers. I’ve also worked a few almost disasters where it was almost impossible to put on a great show.  At those shows I really felt for the customers since I knew if I was having trouble finding water, food, and  good shelter, the patrons must have been miserable. I’ve been doing this for almost 40 years and I don’t work the big hardcore shows anymore. I’m resigned to a handful of smaller bluegrass, Americana, and blues festivals. They are perfect for the old guy I’ve become. I’m too old to sleep on the ground, shiver in the rain, or broil in the heat. The big shows are a young man’s game. (Well, unless you are headlining talent and  I’m not that). That’s alright. I’ve seen just about everything once and a lot of things twice. It’s been a fun ride. 

But I appreciate what it takes to produce one of these large festivals. The organization is amazing and if they pull it off, the rewards can be significant. Millions of dollars can be made or lost. What a gamble.

Author: @krozjr5009
Content: As someone who lived near-ish (10-ish miles?) to the festival site, the stuff at the end about the impact on the roads and railways was really well-researched and spot-on. One interesting fact of note is that — and I don’t know who funded this! — they’ve recently built a second car park at Castle Cary railway station. The original car park was only ever about two-thirds full so this seems like overkill… but during the festival, they’d have no choice but to shut the car park entirely for the shuttle buses, meaning people would park on the streets of the nearby town! Now they have the second car park, the old one still shuts for the buses but the new one is still open — this is vitally important as Castle Cary is also a park-and-ride station for the local area (it was my “local” station despite being a 30 minute drive away, for example). My mum actually drives along the A37 on her way to and from work in the morning, and she avoids the road like the plague during festival weekend! For those who know of the road, choosing the drive along the A303 voluntarily is not a choice she makes lightly! The diversion routes start *miles* away, and they will not let you turn across traffic on the main roads on your exit to speed up traffic flow.

Author: @joeynebulous816
Content:
I worked for a cleaning company during Boomtown (about 120000-140000 people) and did the posh sections (skylark and orchid) which had running hot showers and flushing toilets.

The showers all drained into a massive dug out pit, no lining or anything, then pumped out once a day. At the end of the festival it is filled back in with the dirt that was piled up around it and you could very faintly see a mark on the land where it was. 

The toilets all connected to a pumping/macerating station which then pumped to multiple 10000L storage tanks. All had sight glasses on the side and you could see the level slowly rise with each splash over the course of my 8 hour shifts. The fluid turned from a deep yellow as people woke up to a pale brown as people got hydrated. The tanks were pumped out once or twice a day and there wasn't really as much of a smell as you'd think. The firm that provided the toilets/showers also camped in their caravans behind them.

In the main area the toilets were composting long drops so as you queued up you grab a cup of sawdust, do your drop then drop your sawdust. the pits were above ground so they were collected multiple times a day and the men had long plastic urinals that drained into large vats and yes they did overflow. 

Water was provided by multiple large overland bladders behind the fences in the thicket of trees, these would be full by first thing in the morning and would go down as the day went on, these were fed by 40mm pipes coming out of the ground. I didn't see any water tankers go past so the bladders must have had enough capacity although they did look pretty flat at times. 

The sound systems were ordered to reduce power after a certain time, in 2024 they got it right no one complained about the quietness of the stages after midnight but in previous years people were able to have conversations near the front of the stage. By the time the clock hit midnight on the monday the closing ceremony had finished and all the sound systems had been turned off, only music you could hear was from peoples bluetooth speakers. It was weird not going to sleep with pulsing rolling bass from Tribe of frogs (small stage that ran til 4:30am).

I revisited the site a few months later in the winter and couldn't see any evidence of a festival except a couple of wooden structures that were used as DJ booths, I used the boomtown app map and got my bearings.

A swedish tour I personally worked at had two teams first team would setup the stage in 1-2 days and derig it the very same night as soon as the artist leaves the stage so they have enough time and are on the road asap, while the other team is already on the road to the next location to do the same.

All the instruments were first priority while then detaching all speakers and screens to separate trucks until the stage itself folded into a trailer bed.
